slides.title: Dispatch Copilot: launch it as a Pro tier in Q4 2027, after protecting the mobile rewrite

paragraphs.text: Dispatch Copilot: launch it as a Pro tier in Q4 2027, after protecting the mobile rewrite
Answer to the decision question: Should Brightwork launch Dispatch Copilot in Q2 2027, and if so, how should it be packaged and priced?
Prepared for CEO Maya Okafor and the executive team · Draft of November 2026
Built only from the internal briefing pack. All figures in the pack are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Launch Copilot, but in a per-seat Pro tier, and after the mobile rewrite's next two quarters rather than as a $149 add-on in Q2

paragraphs.text: Launch Copilot, but in a per-seat Pro tier, and after the mobile rewrite's next two quarters rather than as a $149 add-on in Q2

Recommendation: launch Dispatch Copilot inside a new Pro plan at $91 per seat (Core + $12) with a pooled AI allowance, targeting Q4 2027. Keep the mobile team intact through Q2 and use H1 to run a paid pilot on randomly chosen accounts.
The product works for engaged accounts
Beta accounts scheduled 11% more jobs per dispatcher-hour (matched accounts: +2%) and renewed at 97% vs 93%. All 240 were volunteers, so the gain is not yet proven for the wider base.
The prize is $1.2–2.9M of new ARR, not $8M
The 46% "likely to buy" came from the 6% of admins who replied, at larger accounts. When beta accounts were actually asked to pay $149 a month, 14% did.
Price per seat, inside Pro, with a usage pool

A flat $149 add-on attracts the heaviest users: buyers' AI cost is $61 a month. Pro at +$12/seat with 600 requests per seat matches Routewise and holds gross margin at 75% or more. Giving Copilot away in Core would cut margin to ~70%.
Protect mobile first: it is the bigger churn driver
Mobile reliability is the main reason for 27% of churn; AI for 6%. A two-quarter mobile delay loses an estimated $0.5–1.1M ARR for good. A two-quarter Copilot delay puts at most ~$0.6M at risk.
Pro lifts NRR by 2.5–5.0 points once, as accounts migrate. Fixing mobile churn adds 1.9–3.8 points every year. Only the two together reach 105% in the low case.
Bring launch forward to Q2 if the CTO can staff Copilot without the mobile team, or if the Q4 2026 win rate against Routewise fell below 37% with no Routewise discount running.
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Ranges: low case = half the observed rate, high case = observed rate.

slides.title: In the beta, Copilot raised dispatcher productivity and renewals, but every beta account was a volunteer

paragraphs.text: In the beta, Copilot raised dispatcher productivity and renewals, but every beta account was a volunteer
Why the result may not hold for the whole base
Self-selected. All 240 accounts volunteered. Volunteering signals engagement that matching may not remove.
Not typical. Beta accounts average 8.1 seats against 6.2 for the base, and are more active.
Concentrated. The top 10% of beta accounts made 58% of all AI requests.
Short and soft. Hours saved are self-reported. Renewal is measured over 90 days only.
Change in jobs scheduled per dispatcher-hour vs the prior 12 weeks
Beta accounts vs matched non-beta accounts
Beta accounts vs matched non-beta accounts
Self-reported by beta accounts; no comparison group

The signal is real enough to plan a launch. It is not strong enough to assume the same gains, and the same willingness to pay, across 9,800 accounts. A paid pilot on randomly chosen accounts in H1 2027, measured against a control group, settles this before the launch engineering starts.
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Table 1 (240 beta accounts, 12 weeks). Matched non-beta accounts as reported by the product team; matching criteria not stated.

slides.title: Real buying behaviour points to $1.2–2.9M of new ARR in year one, a third or less of the $8M forecast

paragraphs.text: Real buying behaviour points to $1.2–2.9M of new ARR in year one, a third or less of the $8M forecast
New ARR in the first year, $M
Low case: half the observed rate
6% response. 610 of 9,800 admins replied, and they are not typical: 9.4 seats on average vs 6.2 for all accounts.
Intent is not purchase. Offered Copilot at $149 after the free beta, 17 of 120 accounts (14%) bought. Allowing for the small sample, the true rate is plausibly 9–22%.
14% is a ceiling. It comes from volunteer accounts that are larger and more active than the base.
The Pro figure is a precedent, not a test. 33% is how many accounts moved to the 2023 higher tier within a year.
The two realistic options produce similar revenue. They differ on margin and on competitive fit (next two slides).

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), section 6. ARR = 9,800 accounts × adoption × price × 12. Add-on: 7–14% × $149. Pro: 16.5–33% × 6.2 seats × $12. Low case (half the observed rate) is a team assumption.

slides.title: A flat $149 add-on attracts the heaviest users, and for the top tenth AI cost eats almost the whole price

paragraphs.text: A flat $149 add-on attracts the heaviest users, and for the top tenth AI cost eats almost the whole price
AI inference cost per account per month vs the $149 add-on price
Usage scales with account size; a flat price does not. $149 adds 63% to a 3-seat account's $237 Core bill, but under 5% for a 40-seat account.
The add-on's margin is set by its heaviest buyers. At 6,800 requests a month the margin is 59%, below the company's 75% floor.
A per-seat price with a usage allowance ties revenue to usage and caps the downside.
Upside, not assumed: provider list prices fell 35% in the past year; the contract can be renegotiated for 2028.
Buyers used 1.9× the mean account. A flat price draws in the accounts that cost most to serve.

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Table 2 and section 6. AI cost = requests × $0.009 (contract fixed to Dec 2027). Margins are before the $0.6M a year of platform, evaluation and support cost.

slides.title: A Pro tier with a pooled AI allowance beats the $149 add-on on margin safety and fit with Routewise, at similar or higher revenue

paragraphs.text: A Pro tier with a pooled AI allowance beats the $149 add-on on margin safety and fit with Routewise, at similar or higher revenue
Pro tier: +$12 per seat, with usage pool (recommended)
Contribution after AI and platform cost
76.0–76.5%; ≥75% even if every account uses its full pool
Fit with Routewise (AI in its Pro plan)
Matches, but gives the value away
Weaker: AI costs extra and is priced per account
High: flat price; buyers use 1.9× the mean
Capped by the pool; extra use is paid for
Revenue is similar between the two paid options; the Pro tier wins on margin protection, competitive fit and breadth of adoption.

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Contribution = new ARR − AI inference − $0.6M platform cost. Free in Core assumes all accounts at the beta mean of 3,600 requests a month. Engineering: 14 engineers × ½ year × $210k = $1.47M.

slides.title: Without a usage pool, heavy users could pull company gross margin below the 75% floor; with one, it stays above

paragraphs.text: Without a usage pool, heavy users could pull company gross margin below the 75% floor; with one, it stays above
600 requests per seat per month, pooled across the account. The mean beta account used about 444 per seat.
Worst-case AI cost is $5.40 a seat against $12 of extra price, so the uplift keeps at least a 55% margin.
Gross margin stays at 75% or more up to 64% Pro adoption, even if every Pro account uses its whole pool.
Extra requests are sold in packs at a similar margin, so the top tenth of accounts pays for what it uses.
33% adopt, every account at full pool
Upgraders use 6,800 requests, like add-on buyers
All accounts at mean beta usage
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis on $57.6M ARR at 78% gross margin. Includes AI inference at $0.009 per request and $0.6M a year platform cost.

slides.title: Routewise's AI can explain at most a third of the deals Sales expects Copilot to win back

paragraphs.text: Routewise's AI can explain at most a third of the deals Sales expects Copilot to win back
Routewise-contested deals a year that Copilot could win back
Why even the ceiling is generous
Timing. Routewise's AI launched in September, the last month of Q3. Its 20% first-year discount was offered during Q3.
Mentions are not causes. 31% of Q3 loss notes mention AI features. That does not mean AI decided the deal.
Customers rarely leave for AI. "Switched for AI features" is the main reason for only 6% of churned accounts.
The claim exceeds the change. Win-backs can only come from the 7 points of win rate lost since Q2, not from losses that happened before Routewise had AI.
A third of the ~983 deals lost to Routewise
Whole drop in win rate (44% → 37%) caused by AI
A test that is available in January

Q4 2026 is the first full quarter with Routewise's AI on the market. If its discount has ended (Sales to confirm) and the win rate is back near 44%, price drove the drop. If it fell below 37%, the AI gap is widening, and that is a reason to launch in Q2.
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), section 7 and VP Sales memo. 2,600 opportunities × 60% contested = 1,560. New account = 6.2 seats × $79 × 12 = $5,878 ARR.

slides.title: Customers leave over mobile reliability more than four times as often as over AI features

paragraphs.text: Customers leave over mobile reliability more than four times as often as over AI features
Main reason given by accounts that churned in 2026, % of churned accounts
ARR lost a year to mobile reliability (about 370 accounts)
ARR lost a year to AI features (about 80 accounts)
Rank a reliable technician app first, vs AI scheduling, in the 2026 customer survey
The Head of Customer Success is right: mobile is what customers complain about, and what they leave over.

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Table 3 (n = 1,190 churned accounts, 2026) and 2026 customer survey. ARR estimate = 14% logo churn × reason share × $57.6M, assuming churned accounts are average size.

slides.title: Reaching 105% NRR needs both the Pro tier and a mobile fix; neither gets there reliably on its own

paragraphs.text: Reaching 105% NRR needs both the Pro tier and a mobile fix; neither gets there reliably on its own
Range from low case to high case
Pro is a step, not a slope. Once the migration is done, the extra revenue is in the base and stops adding to NRR.
Mobile is the slope. Lower churn raises NRR every year, so it is what keeps 105% after 2028.
Only the pair clears the target in the low case, so the plan must deliver both, in an order that protects the one that compounds.
The $149 add-on gives a similar step (+2.1 to +4.3 pts) with more margin risk.

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Full-year effects; the timing within 2028 depends on when each ships. Mobile: rewrite removes half (low) or all (high) of mobile-driven churn, which is 27% × 14% = 3.8 points of NRR.

slides.title: Delaying the mobile rewrite costs more lasting revenue than delaying Copilot, so mobile should go first

paragraphs.text: Delaying the mobile rewrite costs more lasting revenue than delaying Copilot, so mobile should go first
Proof beyond volunteers: a paid pilot on random accounts measures real uptake, usage and productivity.
A cleaner read on Routewise: two more quarters of win-rate data without its discount.
Cheaper AI at launch: the inference contract runs to December 2027; a Q4 launch spends only one quarter on today's price.
Customer Success's main fear is addressed before Copilot adds support load.
Darker segment: low case. Lighter segment: high case, or the full range where the low end is zero.
It is a close call, and mobile edges it. Accounts lost to churn are gone for good. Pro revenue that starts later is only deferred, and the customers are still there to upgrade.

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Two-quarter slip in each case; we assume a Copilot slip of the same length (CTO to confirm). Copilot figures are upper bounds: they assume AI fully caused the win-rate drop and all AI-driven churn.

slides.title: The offer: Copilot only in a new Pro plan at $91 per seat, with 600 AI requests per seat pooled across the account

paragraphs.text: The offer: Copilot only in a new Pro plan at $91 per seat, with 600 AI requests per seat pooled across the account
No standalone add-on, no Copilot in Core. One way to buy AI keeps the story simple and protects margin.
Per seat, because usage is per seat. A 6.2-seat account pays $74 a month, half the add-on, which widens uptake.
The pool covers typical use. 600 per seat is above the beta mean (~444). Heavy accounts buy packs.
Lead with Pro in Routewise deals, where AI is now included in the rival's top plan.
Move the 17 paying beta accounts to Pro. It costs less than $149 for any account under 12 seats.
Keeps the entry price for price-sensitive accounts (price is 22% of churn)
Dispatch Copilot: AI schedule proposals, quote drafts from technician notes, call summaries
600 AI requests per seat per month, pooled across the account

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Pool size and pack price are team proposals to be tested in the H1 2027 pilot. $20 per 1,000 requests ≈ 55% margin at $0.009 per request.

slides.title: 2027 plan: keep mobile staffed in H1, prove Copilot on a random sample, then launch Pro in Q4

paragraphs.text: 2027 plan: keep mobile staffed in H1, prove Copilot on a random sample, then launch Pro in Q4
Protected: no engineers moved to Copilot
Offer Pro; measure uptake, usage, productivity
Hardening, billing for Pro and usage packs
Gates (red lines): January, check the two triggers for a Q2 launch.  End of Q2, pilot go / no-go before launch engineering starts.
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Assumes the pilot runs on the existing beta platform without the 14-engineer launch team (CTO to confirm).

slides.title: At the end of Q2, four pilot results decide whether Pro launches in Q4 as designed

paragraphs.text: At the end of Q2, four pilot results decide whether Pro launches in Q4 as designed
Pro upgrade rate among randomly offered accounts
At least 16.5% by the end of the pilot
The low case. Below it, Pro brings in under $1.4M ARR and barely covers the $0.6M platform cost.
At least +4.5 points more jobs per dispatcher-hour
Half the beta gap (+11% vs +2%). Shows the gain is not just a volunteer effect.
Median account at or below 600 a month
The pool must cover typical use, or Pro will feel capped and packs will look like a hidden fee.
No worse than the control group
Copilot must not add the reliability complaints that already drive churn.

If a gate is missed: keep Copilot in pilot and rework the offer (pool size, price per seat) before spending the launch engineering. A $149 add-on is not the fallback. Track every quarter after launch: company gross margin (≥75%), win rate against Routewise, Pro adoption against the 16.5–33% range, and mobile rewrite milestones.
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Thresholds are team proposals tied to the low case on earlier slides.

slides.title: Five decisions for the January planning meeting

paragraphs.text: Five decisions for the January planning meeting
Approve Copilot as a Pro tier, not a $149 add-on
$91 per seat (Core + $12), 600 AI requests per seat pooled, extra packs at $20 per 1,000. Target launch: Q4 2027.
Keep the mobile rewrite fully staffed through Q2 2027
No engineers move from mobile to Copilot until the pilot gate at the end of Q2.
Run a paid pilot on ~500 randomly chosen accounts in H1
Offer Pro with a matched control group. 500 accounts give roughly ±3.5 points of precision on the upgrade rate.
Set the two triggers for a Q2 launch now
(a) The CTO can staff Copilot without the mobile team, or (b) the Q4 2026 win rate against Routewise is below 37% with no Routewise discount running.
The current price is fixed to December 2027; provider list prices fell 35% in the past year.
Owners are suggested roles; the briefing pack does not assign them.

slides.title: How the main numbers were calculated

paragraphs.text: How the main numbers were calculated
Beta mean of 3,600 requests per Pro account (cautious: beta accounts are larger)
(0.78 × $57.6M + new ARR − AI cost − $0.6M) ÷ ($57.6M + new ARR)
14% logo churn × reason share × $57.6M; mobile 27% → $2.18M, AI 6% → $0.48M
New ARR ÷ $57.6M; mobile = 27% × 14 pts of churn = 3.8 pts (half fixed = 1.9)
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data). All arithmetic by the team; inputs are as stated in the pack.

slides.title: Choices made where the pack is silent, and what would change the answer

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX B · ASSUMPTIONS AND OPEN QUESTIONS
Choices made where the pack is silent, and what would change the answer
Low case = half the observed rate for both paid options (7% add-on, 16.5% Pro), because the evidence comes from volunteers or a different tier.
Pro accounts use 3,600 requests a month, the beta mean, though beta accounts are larger than average.
The mobile rewrite removes 50–100% of mobile-driven churn. The pack gives no estimate.
Copilot slips by the same two quarters if mobile goes first.
Churned accounts are average size, so churn ARR is proportional to account counts.
Pool of 600 requests and packs at $20 per 1,000 are our design proposals, to be tested in the pilot.
Q4 2026 win rate against Routewise below 37% with no discount running: the AI gap is widening; launch in Q2.
Copilot can be staffed without the mobile team: the trade-off disappears; launch Pro in Q2.
The rewrite fixes little of the mobile churn: delaying mobile costs less; Copilot-first becomes reasonable.
The pilot misses its gates: rework the offer before launch; do not fall back to the $149 add-on.
Beta renewal gain (97% vs 93%) holds for random accounts: Copilot also cuts churn, which strengthens the case for an earlier launch.
The briefing pack was the only input. No questions could be put to the requester; each choice below is the one we would recommend.
